I appreciated the course's progression into general algebraic/topological vector spaces, but I felt the potential of this material was underutilized. Because the examples remained rooted in R^n, the transition to abstract spaces felt like unnecessary complication and a repetition of the first half of the course rather than a powerful tool. As engineering students, I'd like to assume we are already quite comfortable solving finite-dimensional problems using linear algebra. However, we rarely get to practice the heavy calculus required for infinite-dimensional optimization after our freshman year as our curriculums focus heavily on linear algebra and probability/statistics. To truly motivate the second half of the course, I suggest introducing variational problems (e.g., from control theory or other disciplines) instead of standard convex optimization examples. Seeing applications in spaces like L^p would not only justify the theoretical overhead of algebraic/topological vector spaces but also help us strengthen our analysis and calculus skills, which are less emphasized in our other courses as I mentioned.
